Where is Fargo and how big is it?

Fargo is North Dakota's most populous city and the county seat of Cass County, on the western bank of the Red River of the North in the flat Red River Valley. It covers about 50.8 square miles at an elevation of 906 feet.

Across the river is Moorhead, Minnesota, and the Fargo-Moorhead metro is the state's largest urban area. Interstates 29 and 94 intersect in Fargo, with U.S. 10, 52 and 81 also running through. Hector International Airport has the longest public runway in North Dakota, Amtrak's Empire Builder stops at the Fargo station, and MATBUS runs local buses.

Check whether your parcel is in Fargo, West Fargo or unincorporated Cass County before you look up permits or taxes.

What is Fargo's history in brief?

Fargo was founded in 1871, incorporated in 1874 and named for William Fargo, a Northern Pacific Railway director and a founder of Wells Fargo. A fire on June 7, 1893, destroyed 31 downtown blocks, and more than 246 new buildings went up within a year.

North Dakota Agricultural College opened in 1890 and became North Dakota State University in 1960. A tornado in 1957 destroyed much of the north end, and the West Acres Shopping Center opened in 1972. Houses in older parts of the city can differ a great deal from newer ones in age and construction.

How has the Red River shaped selling a house in Fargo?

The Red River sets the rules for a large share of Fargo real estate, because flood risk affects insurance, lending and buyer interest. The National Weather Service recorded a 1997 crest of 39.72 feet at Fargo, 2.42 feet above the 1969 record of 37.3 feet.

Houses bought in flood-prone areas (as of 2012)700

Metro leaders built the FM Area Diversion Project to protect nearly 260,000 people. Its website says permanent flood protection is expected by 2027, and it has pages on land acquisition and flood insurance status. If your Fargo house is near the river, find out whether it is in a mapped floodplain and whether the diversion project affects your parcel before you list. See the FM Diversion site.

What is Fargo's climate and what does it do to a house?

Fargo has very cold winters and warm, humid summers. The January normal mean temperature is 9.2 degrees Fahrenheit, July is 70.7 degrees, and about 43 days a year reach 0 degrees or lower.

  • Average snowfall is 51.4 inches and annual precipitation is 24.0 inches.
  • The average growing season is 144 days.
  • The record low is minus 48 degrees (January 8, 1887) and the record high is 114 degrees (July 6, 1936).

Roof snow load, basement moisture and heating are sensible things to check before listing. If you have had water in the basement, say so and share any repair records.

Who are Fargo's largest employers?

Health care and education lead, alongside food processing, manufacturing and technology, in the Fargo economy, with Sanford Health the largest employer at 6,278 full-time equivalents. The metro's GDP was $18.792 billion in 2022, and the Fargo-Moorhead area has had one of the lowest unemployment rates among U.S. metros since the late 1990s.

West Fargo Public Schools2,541

Fargo Public Schools2,064

NDSU has over 14,500 students and belongs to the Tri-College University system with Minnesota State University Moorhead and Concordia College.

What are Fargo's rental housing inspection rules?

Fargo's Inspections Department enforces the International Property Maintenance Code and Land Development Code Chapter 20 on rental properties, and it asks owners to record their rentals with the department at no charge. If you own a rental you plan to sell, expect the city to have a letter sent to the mailing address on Cass County tax records.

Inspectors look at specific items, and the same items are what a buyer's inspector will flag:

  • Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and deadbolts on entry doors
  • Stair guards, graspable handrails and peeling exterior paint
  • Bathroom and dryer ventilation, window condition and bedroom egress
  • Overcrowding, with a limit of three unrelated tenants

Owners have five business days to change a scheduled inspection date, and unanswered requests can lead to an exterior inspection and fees. The department handles health and safety, not lease or eviction disputes. Details are on the rental housing inspections page.

What are special assessments in Fargo and how do they affect a sale?

Fargo pays contractors as work is built, then pools the cost of projects about once a year and sells a Special Assessment Revenue Bond that property owners repay through yearly special assessment payments. Water main replacement and flood protection are examples of work funded this way.

Owners can look up an address on FargoParcels.com, request a payoff amount through the city's online form, or call the Special Assessment Division at 701.241.1326. The page confirms an annual installment appears on the tax statement but does not say what happens to an assessment at sale, so ask the division and your title company who carries the balance. The city's special assessments page explains the process.

How do Cass County property taxes work for a Fargo sale?

Cass County bills real estate tax on a state schedule: pay in full by February 15 for a 5 percent discount on the consolidated tax, or pay half plus special assessments by March 1 and the rest by October 15. Specials and drain taxes are not discounted.

ItemCass County rule
First installment penalty3% on March 1, May 1, July 1 and October 15
Second installment penalty6% if unpaid after October 15
Prior-year delinquent tax1% interest per month
Tax saleThird Tuesday in November, 10:00 a.m.

The county says all current-year property taxes must be paid in full before a deed transferring ownership can be recorded, and bills go to the owner of record as of November 1. The Finance Office is at the Cass County Courthouse, 211 9th Street South, Fargo, phone (701) 241-5600. Read the Cass County page for payment options.

What should a Fargo seller line up before closing?

Start with the three records that can hold up a Fargo closing: the mortgage payoff, the special assessment balance and the Cass County tax status. Each comes from a different office, so request them early.

  • Payoff letter from your lender.
  • Special assessment payoff amount from the city's Special Assessment Division.
  • Confirmation from the Cass County Finance Office that current-year taxes are paid, since the deed cannot be recorded until they are.
  • Floodplain status for the parcel, and any rental inspection correspondence if the house has tenants.

Having these in hand lets a buyer, cash or financed, move quickly and lets you see what you will net before you commit to a date.

How can a Fargo homeowner sell?

Fargo owners can list, sell privately or accept a cash offer, and the right choice depends on the house and the timeline. A listed sale usually involves repairs, showings and a buyer's loan approval, while a cash purchase takes the house as it stands.

Whichever you pick, North Dakota's disclosure law (Century Code 47-10-02.1) requires sellers of homes with up to four units to disclose material facts, usually before final acceptance of the purchase agreement. We cannot quote a price without seeing the property, and no offer is guaranteed.

More questions about Fargo, ND

How big is Fargo's population?

The Census Bureau estimates 136,275 residents as of July 1, 2025, and the 2020 census counted 125,990.

When did the Red River last set a record at Fargo?

The 2009 crest of 40.84 feet is listed as the record on Wikipedia, above the 1997 NWS crest of 39.72 feet. Check the National Weather Service for current river data.

Do I need to pay off Fargo special assessments before selling?

The city page says you can request a payoff amount but does not say they must be paid at sale. Ask the Special Assessment Division at 701.241.1326 and your title company.

Who gets the Cass County tax bill in a sale?

Bills go to the owner of record as of November 1, and the county advises buyers and sellers to check the closing statement or title company for who pays.

Does Fargo require a rental license?

The inspections page asks owners to ensure rentals are recorded with the department, which is free. It does not describe a license.

Is a cash offer a good idea in Fargo?

It can be when the house needs repairs, is inherited or is a tenant-occupied rental. Compare it with listing costs and timing before you decide.

Where is Bismarck and how is it laid out?

Bismarck is the capital of North Dakota and the county seat of Burleigh County, on the east bank of the Missouri River across from Mandan. The city covers about 36.5 square miles at an elevation of 1,745 feet.

Recent growth has leaned toward the north side, around the shopping centers, while the south side filled in after flood control improved. Older streets near downtown look very different from newer subdivisions, and that gap shows up when a seller tries to price a house. A few points help place an address:

  • The Cathedral District near downtown has some homes dating to the 1880s, with mature American elms along the streets.
  • The south side saw heavy residential and commercial building once Garrison Dam improved flood control in 1953.
  • Interstate 94 crosses the city east to west, and U.S. 83 merges with it in north Bismarck.

Because Mandan sits just across the river in Morton County, a buyer or seller sometimes has to check which county and city a parcel belongs to before looking up taxes or permits.

How did Bismarck get its start?

Settlers founded Bismarck in 1872 at a Missouri River crossing, and the town was incorporated on January 14, 1875. It was first called Edwinton, then renamed in 1873 by the Northern Pacific Railway for Otto von Bismarck.

Gold in the Black Hills in 1874 turned the town into a freight center. Bismarck became the capital of Dakota Territory in 1883 and North Dakota's state capital in 1889. The current Capitol, a 19-story Art Deco tower 241.75 feet tall, was completed in 1934 after the original building burned in 1930.

That history matters to a seller in a practical way. Houses in the oldest blocks may carry original plumbing, knob-and-tube wiring or aging foundations, and those are the repairs that make a traditional listing slow. Newer homes on the north and south edges tend to have different worries, mostly special assessments for streets and utilities.

What does Bismarck's climate mean for a house?

Bismarck has long, windy, snowy winters and warm summers, so roofs, furnaces and insulation get tested every year. The January mean temperature is about 12.8 degrees Fahrenheit, July averages 71.3 degrees, and the record low is minus 45.

Buyers who inspect a Bismarck house usually look hard at the roof, the furnace and the sump pump. A 1879 tornado, the first recorded in North Dakota, is a reminder that spring storms are part of life here. The Upper Missouri still floods seasonally, so anyone near the river should ask about flood zone status before listing.

Source: Bismarck entry on Wikipedia.

Who are the biggest employers in Bismarck?

State government, health care and the school district lead Bismarck's job market. The 2024 employer list shows how concentrated it is.

EmployerEmployees (2024)

Unemployment in the city was 2.6 percent in July 2025, and the 2024 median household income was $73,877. Sellers here often have a job move or retirement date to plan around, and a firm closing date is something a cash sale can sometimes meet.

Which schools, colleges and transit serve Bismarck?

Bismarck Public Schools runs 16 elementary schools, 3 middle schools, 3 public high schools and 1 alternative high school, serving 13,976 students in 2023 to 2024. Families often ask which school a house feeds, so confirm attendance boundaries with the district rather than a listing.

  • University of Mary, a private four-year school
  • Bismarck State College, a public two-year college
  • United Tribes Technical College, a two-year tribal college
  • Bis-Man Transit, which began in 2004 and runs eleven bus routes in Bismarck and Mandan

Bismarck Municipal Airport, south of the city, has the largest passenger volume in western North Dakota. BNSF freight rail crosses town, and passenger rail service ended in 1979.

What are special assessments in Bismarck and who pays them?

A special assessment is a charge for a public improvement that benefits nearby property, and the owner of record pays it with the property tax bill. The city Engineering Department identifies the work and divides the cost among benefiting parcels.

The basis of the charge depends on the improvement:

  • Storm sewer is assessed by lot square footage.
  • Sewer and water are assessed by lot front footage.
  • Paving and street lights are charged per parcel or lot.
  • Sidewalk, curb and gutter are charged by the amount installed.

Owners can pay in full or spread the cost over three to 15 years, depending on the improvement. Each year's installment appears on the tax statement and is paid to the Burleigh County Auditor's Office. When you sell, ask the county for the remaining balance, because a buyer or title company will want it settled or clearly allocated at closing. See the city's special assessments process page.

When are Burleigh County property taxes due for a Bismarck home?

Real estate tax is due January 1, but it can be paid in two installments, March 1 and October 15, or in full by February 15 for a 5 percent discount. The state assessment date for real property is February 1, and county treasurers mail statements on December 26.

DateWhat happens

March 1First installment and special assessments due without penalty
April 1Deadline to apply for the Primary Residence Credit and homestead credit
October 15Second installment due without penalty

Burleigh County accepts payment online, by phone at 1-800-272-9829, or by mail to PO Box 5518, Bismarck, ND 58506-5518. A mailed payment counts as late if it lacks a postmark by the due date, and card payments carry processing fees. Details are on the Burleigh County FAQ and the state deadline calendar.

What must a Bismarck seller disclose?

North Dakota law requires the seller of a home with four units or fewer to disclose material facts that could significantly affect an ordinary buyer's use and enjoyment. When a licensed agent is involved, that means a written form following the Real Estate Commission's format, given before the final purchase agreement is accepted.

Section 47-10-02.1 of the Century Code lists exemptions, including transfers by a fiduciary administering an estate or trust, transfers between close relatives, and foreclosure sales. That is why an inherited Bismarck house often sells with fewer formalities than a listed one. The same section sets no private remedy for buyers, but a licensee who ignores it can be disciplined by the Real Estate Commission. See the statute at ndlegis.gov.

North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax, according to the Grand Forks County Recorder, which keeps a closing here cheaper in one respect than in many states.

What are the ways to sell a house in Bismarck?

A Bismarck homeowner can list with an agent, sell privately, or sell to a cash buyer, and each route trades time against price and certainty. Listing usually asks for repairs, showings and weeks of waiting on a buyer's loan.

  • List with an agent when the house is in good shape and you can wait for a mortgage buyer.
  • Sell privately when you already have a buyer and are comfortable with the paperwork.
  • Take a cash offer when the house needs work, is inherited, is tenant-occupied or has a deadline.

With a cash sale, the buyer takes the house as it stands, and the seller does not coordinate repairs or open houses. Whichever route you choose, order a payoff statement for any mortgage, find your special assessment balance, and check the county tax record before you set a closing date. Offers depend on the property, so we make no promise on price or timing before we see the house.

More questions about Bismarck, ND

Does Bismarck have a state income tax or transfer tax on home sales?

North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax, according to the Grand Forks County Recorder's page. Ask a tax professional about federal income tax on any gain, since that is separate.

Who pays Burleigh County property tax when a house sells?

The statement goes to the owner of record, and the closing statement decides how the year is divided between buyer and seller. The Burleigh County FAQ does not cover proration, so ask your title company.

Can I sell a Bismarck house that still has special assessments?

Yes. Installments run three to 15 years and appear on the tax statement, so the balance is paid off at closing or carried by the buyer as the contract states.

Do I need a seller disclosure form in Bismarck?

If a licensed agent is involved, you must prepare a written disclosure before the buyer signs the final acceptance. Without an agent, you must still disclose material facts in writing. Estates and some family transfers are exempt.

How cold does Bismarck get, and does that affect selling?

January averages about 12.8 degrees and the record low is minus 45. Buyers check the furnace, insulation and roof closely, so a house with old heating tends to draw lower bids.

What if I inherited a Bismarck house and live elsewhere?

You can sell it as it is. Gather the death certificate, the county tax record and any assessment balance, and ask an attorney about probate before signing a deed.

Where is Grand Forks and why is it called that?

Grand Forks is the county seat of Grand Forks County, on the western bank of the Red River of the North where the Red Lake River joins it. It sits at 837 feet and covers about 29.3 square miles, 74 miles north of the Fargo-Moorhead area and 145 miles south of Winnipeg.

French fur traders called the site Les Grandes Fourches, and a U.S. post office opened on June 15, 1870, under the English name. Steamboat captain Alexander Griggs, who wintered here in 1870 after his boat froze in, platted the community in 1875. The city was incorporated on February 22, 1881.

The area is one of the flattest regions in the world and the city has no lakes within its limits.

How did the 1997 flood change Grand Forks?

The April 1997 Red River flood devastated the city and led to a new levee system and a greenway where homes once stood. The National Weather Service recorded a crest of 54.35 feet at East Grand Forks on April 22, 1997, against a flood stage of 28 feet and a previous record of 48.8 feet from 1979.

1997 flood factFigure

Downtown buildings destroyed by fire, April 1911, including 60 apartments

The two sources give different damage totals, since one counts the entire Red River basin event and the other the greater Grand Forks area. A new levee system was completed about ten years later, requiring the relocation of numerous residents, and the old floodplain became the Greater Grand Forks Greenway. Ask your insurer and the city about flood zone status for any house near the river. Sources: the National Weather Service and NBC News.

How did Grand Forks grow to its current size?

Grand Forks grew from 1,705 residents in 1880 to 59,166 in the 2020 census, helped by railroads that arrived early. The Great Northern Railway came in 1880 and the Northern Pacific in 1887, and UND opened in 1883, six years before statehood.

The North Dakota Mill and Elevator, built in the 1920s, is described as the nation's largest flour mill, and the Air Force base brought thousands of jobs after 1954. Wikipedia gives an estimated 59,845 residents in 2024, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 60,365, so the city is growing slowly.

What is the economy like in Grand Forks?

Higher education, defense and health care dominate Grand Forks, with the University of North Dakota the city's largest employer at 5,562 workers. The economy also includes manufacturing, food processing and scientific research.

EmployerEmployees
University of North Dakota5,562

Notable manufacturers include LM Wind Power, which makes wind turbine blades, and Cirrus Design, which builds light aircraft. The Air Force Base, selected as a site in 1954, lies just west of the city. UND, founded in 1883, is the state's oldest higher education institution and the only home of its medical and law schools.

Owners who rented to students, faculty or service members may be selling after a tenant move rather than on a schedule they chose.

What is the climate in Grand Forks?

Grand Forks has a warm-summer humid continental climate in USDA hardiness zone 4a, and subfreezing temperatures have occurred in every month of the year. Annual precipitation averages about 21.7 inches and snowfall about 48.4 inches.

  • Record low: minus 43 degrees Fahrenheit on January 11, 1912.
  • Record high: 109 degrees on July 12, 1936.
  • A deadly tornado in 1887 killed at least six people.

Basement moisture and sump pump function are sensible items to check before listing. If your house took water in a recent spring, keep invoices and photos for the buyer.

What roads, transit and schools serve Grand Forks?

Interstate 29, U.S. 2, U.S. 81 and ND 297 serve Grand Forks, and the city's transit system, Cities Area Transit, has run since 1926 with 12 routes. Grand Forks International Airport has Delta flights to Minneapolis-St. Paul and Allegiant service, and Amtrak's Empire Builder stops at the Grand Forks station.

Grand Forks Public Schools is the largest school employer in the city at about 1,700 workers. Because school attendance areas can change, confirm a house's school assignment with the district before quoting it to buyers.

What are Grand Forks' rental inspection rules?

Grand Forks requires a Certificate of Occupancy for rental units whether or not rent is collected, and one- and two-family rentals have faced a licensing requirement since 2006. The city inspects each rental about every five years, or sooner after complaints.

The inspection checklist is specific. Items include:

  • Heating that keeps each occupied room at 68 degrees, three feet above the floor.
  • At least two off-street parking spaces, with more depending on bedroom count.
  • Smoke detectors, egress, electrical wiring and handrails or guardrails to the code in effect when the building was built.
  • No more than four unrelated individuals per unit.
  • Junk or junk vehicles resolved before a certificate issues.

Non-compliant owners can be cited in municipal court, and a judge may order a unit vacated. See the rental inspections program page.

What does the Grand Forks County Recorder do in a sale?

The Grand Forks County Recorder's Office records documents that affect title to real property, such as a deed, and keeps them permanently. It is at 151 South 4th Street, and the phone is 701-780-8262.

The office's page states that North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax. Copies cost $1.00 per page, and certified copies cost $5.00 for the first page and $2.00 for each additional page. The page does not list recording fees, so ask the office or your title company. See the Recorder's Office.

Under North Dakota's disclosure law, a seller of a home with up to four units must disclose material facts in writing, and sales by a mortgagor in default, foreclosure sales and transfers by estate fiduciaries are exempt. Read Century Code 47-10-02.1.

Can I sell my Grand Forks house if I am behind on payments?

Yes, a sale is possible at any stage before a foreclosure sale, and North Dakota's process gives you time to act. Foreclosure is judicial, the lender must usually give 30 to 90 days' notice before suing, and the borrower has 30 days from notice to reinstate.

Nolo's summary of the statutes says redemption after sale generally lasts 60 days, and deficiency judgments are barred for owner-occupied residential property of four or fewer units on up to 40 contiguous acres. The federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act gives added protection to military personnel, which matters near the base. Review Nolo's guide and speak to an attorney.

If you want a quick sale, a cash offer buys the house as it stands, and we make no promise of a price before seeing it. Compare it with listing, factoring in repairs, commissions and time.

More questions about Grand Forks, ND

How many people live in Grand Forks?

The Census Bureau estimates 60,365 residents as of July 1, 2025. The 2020 census counted 59,166.

Is Grand Forks still at risk of flooding?

A new levee system was completed about ten years after 1997, and the old floodplain became the Greenway. Ask the city and your insurer about your parcel.

Does Grand Forks require rental licensing?

One- and two-family rentals have been subject to a licensing requirement since 2006, and every rental needs a Certificate of Occupancy.

Is there a deed tax when I sell a Grand Forks house?

The County Recorder's page says North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax. Recording and title fees are separate.

What happens if I miss mortgage payments in Grand Forks?

The lender usually sends a notice 30 to 90 days before filing suit and you have 30 days to pay the past-due amount. A judge must approve a foreclosure sale.

When are Grand Forks County property taxes due?

Statewide, real estate tax can be paid in full by February 15 for a 5 percent discount, or in installments due March 1 and October 15. Confirm county details with the Treasurer.

Where is Minot, North Dakota, and what are its main areas?

Minot is a north-central North Dakota city in Ward County, on the Drift Prairie about 110 miles north of Bismarck. The Mouse River, also called the Souris River, runs through it from west to east and splits the city roughly in half.

Locals describe three areas. North Hill is the plateau north of the river valley, the Mouse River Valley holds downtown and the older neighborhoods along the water, and South Hill is the broad area to the south. The valley sits about 160 feet below the surrounding plains, with the river at about 1,540 feet above sea level at city center. The Census Bureau estimates 47,308 residents as of July 1, 2025.

How did Minot get its start?

Minot came into existence in 1886 when the Great Northern Railway laid track through the area, and a tent town appeared almost overnight. Population passed 5,000 within five months, which earned the city its nickname, the Magic City.

The Soo Line reached Minot in 1893. In the 1950s federal money arrived with Minot Air Force Base, built in 1956 and 1957 about 13 miles north of town, and Garrison Dam on the Missouri River, finished in 1953. Later growth came from oil drilling in the Bakken Formation, which Wikipedia credits with population and infrastructure investment across the region.

For a seller, those layers mean a wide range of housing ages. Homes built over more than a century sell under the same city rules but can have very different repair needs.

Why does the Mouse River matter to a Minot house sale?

The Mouse River is the single biggest factor in how buyers and insurers look at a Minot property in or near the valley. A flood in April 1969 devastated the city, and the Army Corps of Engineers afterward straightened the river's path and built flood control structures.

The 2011 flood was larger. On June 26, 2011 the river crested at 1,561.7 feet, three feet above the previous record set in 1881. About 12,000 people were evacuated. According to Wikipedia's summary, more than 4,100 homes were affected, 2,376 of them extensively, and 805 were damaged beyond repair. North Dakota's Department of Emergency Services reported that the existing flood control system had been designed for flows of up to 5,000 cubic feet per second, and that the June 2011 flows exceeded 27,400 cubic feet per second.

  • The Mouse River Enhanced Flood Protection Project began in 2011 and is meant to reduce flood risk across the whole basin.
  • FEMA has been developing new flood insurance rate maps for the Mouse River Basin in response to the 2011 flood.
  • Project updates describe ongoing construction in downtown Minot under a phase labeled MI-6, along the east Central Avenue corridor.

If your home flooded, was repaired or was bought out in past years, keep every record. Three U.S. highways meet in Minot. US 2 is a four-lane divided highway running east to Grand Forks and west toward Williston, US 83 runs north to the Minot Air Force Base and south to Bismarck, and US 52 runs southeast toward Jamestown and northwest to the Canadian border at Portal.

A city ordinance item posted on the Minot agenda center states that if the city corrects a code violation, the cost is levied as a special assessment against the property. What must a Minot seller disclose, and what are the selling options?

North Dakota law requires written disclosure of material facts in most residential sales. N.D.C.C. 47-10-02.1 applies to dwellings with up to four units, requires the seller to complete the form in good faith before the buyer signs final acceptance, and lists exceptions such as foreclosure sales and sales by a fiduciary administering an estate. Section 47-10-02.2 adds a written radon disclosure for residential property.

What river runs through Minot?

The Mouse River, also called the Souris River, runs through Minot from west to east and divides the city roughly in half. It flooded badly in 1969 and again in June 2011, and a basin-wide flood protection project that began in 2011 is still underway.

Is Minot Air Force Base the largest employer in the area?

A city ordinance item on the Minot agenda center says the cost to correct a violation can be levied as a special assessment against the property. Resolve any open complaint, or ask the Building Safety division what is outstanding, before you sell.

West Fargo started as a whistle stop on the Northern Pacific Railway called Sheyenne Crossing, named for the nearby Sheyenne River. The city is home to Dickinson State University and a Ukrainian Cultural Institute with a museum. Figures like these come from survey estimates, so treat them as a general picture rather than a forecast for any single street.

What are property taxes like for a Dickinson home?

Stark County's 2026 levy figures show Dickinson's school district levy at $27,215,460.41 and the city's levy at $6,060,550.00, part of a county total of $14,002,779.90. These are dollar amounts raised, not mill rates, so your bill depends on your parcel's taxable value.

Tax dates follow the state calendar: statements are mailed December 26, the 5 percent discount ends February 15, the first installment is due March 1 and the second October 15. The Primary Residence Credit, worth up to $1,600 applied to the next year's tax, requires an application by March 31, and the state lists April 1 as the deadline. Homestead credit applications go to the local assessor.

Stark County recommends contacting the Auditor's office, the County Tax Director or the Dickinson City Assessor for forms. See the Stark County 2026 budget insert and the state calendar.

What if I am behind on the mortgage on a Dickinson house?

North Dakota foreclosures go through the courts, and the lender must usually send a notice 30 to 90 days before filing suit, giving you 30 days to pay what is past due. After a foreclosure sale, a borrower generally has 60 days to redeem, except for abandoned or agricultural property, according to Nolo's summary of N.D.C.C. 32-19-18.

The same summary says deficiency judgments are prohibited for foreclosures of residential property of four units or fewer, one of which the owner occupies, on up to 40 contiguous acres. Selling before a sale date is one way to settle the loan on your own terms. Read the full Nolo guide and talk to an attorney or a HUD-approved counselor before you decide.

Is a cash sale a good fit for a Dickinson house?

A cash sale can fit when the house needs repairs, is inherited, is rented or has a deadline, because the buyer purchases it as it stands and no lender appraisal is involved. It does not suit every owner, and a well-kept house with time on its side may do better on the open market.

  • Ask what costs each route carries, including agent commission, repairs and carrying costs.
  • Get your mortgage payoff and any special assessment balance in writing.
  • Confirm who will pay the current year's property tax at closing.

North Dakota requires sellers of homes up to four units to disclose material facts in writing, but fiduciaries administering an estate or trust are exempt under Century Code 47-10-02.1. Our team will tell you what we can and cannot say about price until we have seen the house.

More questions about Dickinson, ND

How many people live in Dickinson?

The Census Bureau estimates 25,870 residents as of July 1, 2025, and the 2020 census counted 25,679, up about 44 percent from 17,787 in 2010.

What schools serve Dickinson?

Dickinson Public Schools operates six elementary schools, a junior high, Dickinson High School and an alternative high school. Parochial options include Dickinson Trinity and Hope Christian Academy, and Dickinson State University is in the city.

When are Stark County property taxes due?

Statements are mailed December 26. Paying in full by February 15 earns a 5 percent discount. Otherwise the first installment is due March 1 and the second October 15.

Can I sell a Dickinson house that was damaged in a storm?

Yes. A 2009 EF3 tornado damaged more than 450 homes and businesses here, so buyers know the pattern. Keep your insurance claim records and photographs.

How long do I have to redeem a Dickinson home after foreclosure?

North Dakota generally allows 60 days after the sale, except for abandoned or agricultural property, according to Nolo's summary of the statute. Confirm the dates for your case with an attorney.

Do I need a seller disclosure in Dickinson?

Yes for most sales of homes with up to four units, either on a written form when an agent is involved or in writing otherwise. Estate fiduciaries and some family transfers are exempt.

Where is Mandan, North Dakota, and how is the city laid out?

Mandan sits on the west bank of the Missouri River, directly across from Bismarck, on the eastern edge of Morton County. It is the county seat and one of the two core cities of the Bismarck metropolitan area.

The city covers about 13.7 square miles at an elevation of roughly 1,647 feet. The Census Bureau counted 24,206 residents in 2020 and estimates 25,061 for July 1, 2025, which makes Mandan the eighth-most populous city in North Dakota. Interstate 94, Interstate 194 and North Dakota highways 6 and 1806 serve the city.

What is the history behind Mandan's neighborhoods?

Mandan began as a Northern Pacific Railroad work camp in December 1878 and took its present name when the post office returned to it in September 1879. On March 3, 1879 the post office moved to the railroad's city site, within blocks of the first depot at Main Street and Stark Avenue, which is today's Collins Avenue.

The land has a much longer record. A Mandan village known as Good Fur Robe stood at the base of Crying Hill and was recorded as early as 1738, and the city takes its name from the Mandan people, who are now part of the Three Affiliated Tribes. In 1873 the Army added a cavalry post at Fort Abraham Lincoln, about five miles south of the townsite. The fort was deactivated in 1892 and the site is now Fort Abraham Lincoln State Park.

A rail division headquarters opened in Mandan in 1881, and BNSF still runs the railroad facilities. For a seller, the practical point is that Mandan has a long-settled core, so the age of a house and of its wiring, plumbing and heating can vary a lot from block to block.

What does Mandan's climate mean for a house?

Mandan has a humid continental climate with large swings between seasons, and a buyer or inspector will look closely at the roof, the furnace and the foundation. Records since 1913 show a high of 115 degrees Fahrenheit in July and a low of minus 46 in both February and December.

  • January afternoons average about 22.5 degrees and nights about 2.7 degrees, so heating systems carry most of the winter load.
  • Average yearly precipitation is about 18.4 inches, with June the wettest month at roughly 3.4 inches.

Mandan's building department lists furnace changeouts and water heater changeouts among the jobs that need a permit. If you replaced either one without a permit, expect the question to come up when a buyer's inspector asks for paperwork.

Climate figures come from the 1991 to 2020 normals reproduced on Wikipedia.

Do I need permits to be in good shape for a Mandan sale?

You do not need a permit to sell, but unpermitted work is the most common thing that slows a Mandan sale once a buyer starts asking questions. The city's Building Department (701-667-3230) says a permit is required before work starts, and it explains the reason in terms of selling: a history of construction matters when you sell, refinance or insure a home.

According to the city's permit FAQ, a permit is required for:

  • any structural alteration, residential or commercial
  • residential construction exceeding $2,000
  • window replacements that change the window size
  • any structure larger than 120 square feet
  • furnace changeouts, water heater changeouts and fireplace installs
  • water and sewer hookups

Permits are not required for painting, carpeting, tiling, countertops, fences up to 8.5 feet, or swimming pools. A permit usually takes under an hour to issue, and inspections carry no extra charge. The city also tells owners to check any contractor's license through the North Dakota Secretary of State, which is worth doing before you pay for repairs ahead of a sale.

How do special assessments work when I sell a house in Mandan?

A special assessment is a charge the city levies on property that benefits from a public project, and an unpaid balance follows the property into a sale. Mandan uses assessments for street paving, water and sewer mains, sidewalks, curb and gutter, and also for weed cutting, snow removal and diseased tree removal.

The city's special assessment page lays out the process. Costs for water, sewer and street projects are generally spread over 15 years, while repairs to private water or sewer lines and tree removal are typically spread over five. Weed cutting and delinquent utility bills carry a 10 percent administrative fee. The city auditor certifies each year's installment to the county by November 1, and owners can pay without interest through February 15 of the following year.

  • Search an address or parcel on the city's Special Assessment Inquiry Dashboard. If the parcel does not appear, there are no specials on it.
  • Call 701-667-3271 for payoff figures, or visit the Auditor's Office at 205 2nd Avenue NW.
  • For rural parcels outside city limits, Morton County handles balances at 701-667-3326.

Ask for the payoff figure before you accept any offer, because the amount is deducted from your proceeds at closing.

How is property tax calculated and paid on a Mandan home?

Morton County bills the tax, and the state sets the formula. The assessor first sets a true and full value, which for a home is market value. Assessed value is 50 percent of that, and the taxable value for residential property is 4.5 percent of the true and full value.

The State Tax Commissioner's residential property tax page gives a worked example: a $275,000 home in an area with 250 total mills has a taxable value of $12,375 and owes $3,095. Your own levy depends on the city, school district and other taxing entities that cover your parcel.

The county notes that failing to receive a bill does not remove the obligation to pay. Credits for primary residence, homestead and disabled veterans are listed on the state's residential page, and it is worth claiming one before a sale if you still qualify.

What do I have to disclose, and how does Mandan recording work?

North Dakota requires written disclosures from sellers, and the rules depend on who is involved in the sale. Under N.D.C.C. 47-10-02.1, a seller of a residential dwelling with up to four units must give the buyer a written disclosure of material facts before the buyer signs final acceptance. Sales by a fiduciary administering an estate, sales through foreclosure, and transfers to close family are among the exceptions.

  • Radon: section 47-10-02.2 requires you to disclose in writing what you know about radon concentrations and to hand over any past test results or mitigation records.
  • Homeowners associations: section 47-10-02.3 requires association documents and fee information within ten days of signing.
  • Deeds: section 47-10-07 requires each deed to contain the post office address of every grantee.

The Morton County Recorder files the deed and keeps the land records that feed the county's tax rolls. The office also runs a free Property Fraud Alert that notifies an owner whenever a document is recorded against a property. Read the statute text at the North Dakota legislature's Title 47 chapter 10.

What are my options for selling a Mandan house quickly?

Mandan sellers generally choose among three routes: list with an agent, sell the house yourself, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who purchases as-is. Each has a different timeline and a different set of costs that fall on you.

A traditional listing can reach the widest buyer pool, but it usually involves showings, inspection requests and financing that depends on an appraisal. A cash purchase removes the lender step, and the buyer takes the house in its present condition, which suits a home with deferred maintenance, an unpermitted addition, or a tenant in place. If you are weighing a cash offer, compare the net amount you would receive after payoff of any special assessments, taxes and liens, not just the headline number.

Cash Home Buyers does not promise a price on this page. We can review a Mandan address and explain how an offer would be built, and you owe nothing if you turn it down.

More questions about Mandan, ND

Is Mandan the county seat of Morton County?

Yes. Mandan was designated the county seat in 1881, and the county courthouse and the Recorder, Treasurer and Tax Equalization offices are in the city. That means deed recording and property tax questions for a Mandan house are handled in your own city.

When are Mandan property taxes due?

Morton County mails statements each December, and the State Tax Commissioner says real property tax is payable without penalty until March 1. A 5 percent discount applies when the consolidated tax is paid in full by February 15, and a postmark counts as proof of timely payment.

Do I need a permit to replace a furnace or water heater in Mandan?

Yes. The Mandan Building Department lists furnace and water heater changeouts among the work that requires a permit. Call 701-667-3230 if you are unsure about another project.

Who pays special assessments when a Mandan house is sold?

The balance is tied to the parcel, and who pays it at closing depends on the purchase contract, so settle that in writing. Request a payoff from the city Auditor's Office at 701-667-3271 before you accept an offer.

Do I have to give a buyer a disclosure form in North Dakota?

For a residential dwelling of up to four units, yes in most sales. N.D.C.C. 47-10-02.1 requires a written disclosure of material facts, and 47-10-02.2 adds a radon disclosure. Estate fiduciaries, foreclosure sales and certain family transfers are exempt from the main disclosure form.

Can I sell a Mandan house with unpermitted work?

You can, but a buyer or lender may ask for documentation. A buyer that purchases as-is decides whether to accept the risk, and you should still tell the buyer what you know about the work.
